analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover autoimmune and blood disorder drugs and limits prior authorization to once a year.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 8, 2026 with one Republican cosponsor and sent to three House committees, where it has had no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force group and individual health plans to cover any drug prescribed for an autoimmune disease, hemophilia, or Von Willebrand disease, whether dispensed by a pharmacy or given in a clinic. It would also bar plans from requiring prior authorization—getting the insurer's approval before a drug is covered—more than once every 12 months for these drugs, with narrow exceptions for opioids, sedatives, and drugs under an FDA safety program. The changes would take effect for plan years starting January 1, 2027.
analysis.who_benefits: People with lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, multiple sclerosis, inflammatory bowel disease, hemophilia, Von Willebrand disease, and similar conditions. Millions of Americans take these drugs, which are often expensive specialty medicines, and today many must get insurer approval repeatedly, sometimes waiting days and going without medication.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients with autoimmune and bleeding disorders

how_it_helps.text: Plans must cover any drug indicated for an autoimmune disease, hemophilia, or Von Willebrand disease, whether from a pharmacy or in a clinical setting.
Plans may not require prior authorization for these drugs more than once in any 12-month period, so patients no longer need fresh approval for ongoing treatment each cycle.

The rules apply to group plans under ERISA and the tax code and to group and individual insurance under the Public Health Service Act, closing the gap where self-insured employer plans are governed separately.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers who fund group plans would bear higher drug spending, since they could no longer use repeated prior authorization to slow or block the costliest specialty drugs. Some of that cost would likely flow back into premiums for all enrollees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: The bill mandates coverage of all indicated autoimmune and blood disorder drugs, which include some of the most expensive biologics in medicine, without any provision to restrain their list prices, so plan and premium costs could rise.
It guarantees coverage but says nothing about out-of-pocket costs, deductibles, or co-payments, so a patient may get the drug approved faster and still not be able to afford it.

Insurers argue prior authorization exists to prevent misuse and steer patients to cheaper alternatives; limiting it to once a year removes that check for drugs patients take indefinitely, even if prescribing patterns change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients whose treatment has been delayed or interrupted by repeated insurer approvals, the benefit is immediate and personal. The honest tradeoff is money: requiring coverage and limiting utilization management for high-cost specialty drugs will add to plan spending, and none of that new cost is offset by drug-price controls or out-of-pocket relief, so part of it lands back on the same people through premiums.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and split among three House committees, none of which has taken it up, so it sits waiting with no hearing or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Representative Julie Johnson of Texas introduced the bill on June 8, 2026, joined by Representative Mike Lawler, a Republican, as its sole cosponsor.

The same day, the Speaker referred it to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Education and Workforce, and Ways and Means, meaning three different committees would each have to act on their piece before the full House could consider it.
No hearing, markup, or floor action has occurred since the referral, and the bill has just one cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers and pharmacy benefit managers keep their current authority to require repeated prior authorization, because the bill has not advanced. Patients with autoimmune and bleeding disorders continue to face the approval hurdles the bill would have removed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and PBMs keep the status quo

sides.party_line_note: A Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor gave it bipartisan backing at introduction, but no one has opposed it on the record because no committee or floor vote has occurred.

industries.note: Insurers would have to cover every indicated autoimmune and blood disorder drug and could require prior authorization only once a year, giving up their main tool for managing spending on the costliest specialty drugs. Their loss of discretion is the patient's gain in access.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and utilization-management vendors
industries.note: These firms administer prior authorization for insurers; capping it at once a year shrinks the volume of review work and the leverage they hold over prescribing.

industries.industry: Brand-name biologic and specialty drug makers
industries.note: The bill guarantees coverage of drugs indicated for autoimmune and blood disorders, a category dominated by high-priced biologics, without touching their prices. Patients get faster access to these drugs, and the makers get a guaranteed covered market.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has one cosponsor, three committee referrals, and no scheduled action. Most House bills referred to three committees die without a hearing, and with no clear committee champion, its realistic path is that it ends the Congress without a vote unless it is folded into a broader health package.
